https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: People pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images Thailand Thailand suspends gun licences as teen shooter and grandparents he killed are cremated Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul calls for tighter gun controls and ‘decisive penalties’ after nine dead in school shooting Natasha May in Bangkok and agencies Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.28 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thailand has suspended firearms licences after the deadly Nonthaburi school shooting , as the bodies of the teenage attacker and the grandparents he killed were cremated. The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, said he had ordered the interior ministry and police to stop issuing licences to possess, purchase and carry firearms, and called for “tighter controls and decisive penalties”. The measures are temporary until a new gun control law is in place, according to government operated news-channel NBT World. Anutin had vowed to implement changes on Friday when earlier that morning a 14-year-old boy shot dead the grandparents who raised him at their home in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, before killing six others at his school and then turning the gun on himself. At a temple in Thailand, parents mourn a 12-year-old mass shooting victim, and a father pleads for forgiveness Read more Anutin had aimed for reforms in previous roles as minister for the interior and health after gun violence in 2022 and 2023. In 2023, a shooting saw a boy of the same age kill two people at a shopping mall using a modified pistol intended to fire blanks that police said was likely ordered online. Anutin ordered a raft of gun control measures, including a short-term ban on new licences, import restrictions and the banning of people under 20 years old from shooting ranges. However, past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented recent shootings. While Thailand’s licensing laws appear tough on paper, the reality is the country has millions of unregistered guns. The most recent data from the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey in 2017 showed that with over 10m civilian-owned firearms, Thailand had the highest number in south-east Asia – a rate more than one gun for every seven people – and over 4m were unregistered. The government plans to establish a designated period for people to surrender illegal firearms or inherited weapons that cannot be legally transferred, during which they may be exempt from penalties, according to government operated news-channel NBT World. Commissioner General Kitrat Phanphet of the Royal Thai police has also ordered tighter oversight of government-issued police firearms. The widely criticised “welfare gun” scheme allows eligible public officials to obtain weapons at steep discounts, but the Bangkok Post reports many of these guns end up being resold. Deputy Commissioner General Thana Chuwong will be responsible for targeting illegal weapons possession and trafficking, including illegal weapons sales through social media and other online platforms. A new school safety plan has also been introduced by the ministry of education, including stricter entry screening with guards to check for weapons before anyone enters school premises, and increased mental health counselling. View image in fullscreen The wife of a teacher killed in the Debsirin Nonthaburi school shooting weeps. Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA The reforms were foreshadowed as multi-day Buddhist funerals for the victims continued to take place. The white caskets of the first victims, the shooter’s grandparents, were laid out at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple on Tuesday, alongside their portraits, ahead of their cremation capping a funeral lasting several days. The boy’s smaller casket was placed to the side at the same temple, surrounded by white flowers. Among the mourners was Tawee Piewphong, who paid tribute to his brother-in-law – the grandfather – as “a man of few words, but a very kind person”. Tawee expressed shock at the killings, saying he had no idea what motivated the teenager, but also offered compassion. “I want to tell him that being 14 is just a small fraction of your entire life, and every problem has a solution. Not everything is the end of the world,” the 70-year-old said. Investigators were still seeking a motive for the shooting, but police said on Sunday that the boy had watched violent videos online and once brought an air gun to school. Officials said previously that he faced academic-related stress, and a classmate said he was bullied. “Of course I feel bad for the innocent people who were killed,” said Somjai Poosod, whose grandchildren attend the school attacked. “But I feel there is an issue of mental health that we may need to address to prevent incidents like this from happening again.” The shooting has resonated across the country, with the king and Anutin leading an outpouring of grief. On Monday, the attacker’s father told the Guardian he still did not understand why his son did it, but was left to reckon with the violence his own flesh and blood had committed. “I’m experiencing so many emotions all at once. I feel guilty and heartbroken because I’ve suffered a loss too. I’ve lost my child, as well as my parents.” The shooter used his grandfather’s gun to kill his grandparents before heading to the school. There, he shot dead five teachers and staff and wounded a 12-year-old girl who died in hospital on Saturday. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-prison-for-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IyFn Lev Shlosberg has maintained his innocence and called for an immediate end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine Image: Olga Maltseva/AFP Advertisement Lev Shlosberg, a senior member of Russia 's liberal opposition party Yabloko, was pronounced guilty of "public actions aimed at discrediting the use of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation" and sentenced to 11 years and 1 month in a penal colony by a court in Pskov on Monday. Shlosberg has described the war as a catastrophe for Russia. The Kremlin says he is spreading slanderous lies about the army. Making his closing statement before the verdict and sentence were read on Monday, Shlosberg maintained his innocence, saying he was the victim of a political trial. On August 10, Russia's Supreme Court banned Yabloko — the only registered political party calling for an end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine — from participating in upcoming parliamentary elections . The decision was upheld on Monday. What did Shlosberg say about Russia's war in Ukraine? During his closing statement, Shlosberg repeated his call for an immediate ceasefire in the four-and-a-half-year war in neighboring Ukraine. "The lives of countless thousands of people have been cut short during this time. Sooner or later, the precise and complete death toll — with names included — will be made public, and the entire nation will shudder at this list of martyrs," he said, according to ‌a transcript. BBC's Russia Service and the independent Russian media outlet Mediazona say they have counted the names of more than 239,354 fallen Russian soldiers via public records. However, when they factored in death certificates and estate information to arrive at excess mortality numbers they topped 350,000. Russia does not publish casualty figures. Russian opposition leads first major anti-war march abroad To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Kremlin and courts snuffing out all public opposition to war Public criticism of the war, which the Kremlin says is not a war but rather a "special military operation," is practically non-existent inside Russia as a result of draconian laws stifling speech related to it. In the wake of the February 24, 2022, invasion, Russia's parliament passed laws to punish anyone found guilty of "discrediting" the army or deliberately "spreading false information" about the operation with long jail sentences. Shlosberg was arrested last year on charges that he had "discredited" the military during a video debate, referring to the war in Ukraine as a "bloody game of chess." The charge of spreading fake news about the war was added after he reposted the video on Telegram. "A single person is imprisoned, yet fear seeps into the hearts of millions," said Shlosberg in his closing remarks. Shlosberg is the second person from his party to feel the heel of state justice of late. In June, deputy Yabloko party leader, Maxim Kruglov, was sentenced to seven years in prison "for spreading lies about Russia's military." https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/german-polic.text: Europe German police report sabotage attack on power grid near Cologne ‘Based on current state of investigation, we do not believe this was technical malfunction, but rather deliberate act — a criminal offense,’ police spokesperson says Oliver Towfigh Nia 02 September 2026 • Update : 02 September 2026 BERLIN An electric substation near Cologne was the target of a sabotage attack, police said Wednesday. “Based on the current state of the investigation, we do not believe this was a technical malfunction, but rather a deliberate act— a criminal offense,” a police spokesperson for the western city of Essen told the German Press Agency. The cause and circumstances of the incident in the Rhein-Erft district remain unclear. The investigation is in full swing. According to the spokesperson, the police were called to the substation in the Rheidt district of Bergheim around 8 pm local time (1800GMT) on Tuesday evening due to a technical malfunction. A short circuit caused several power lines to fail. Based on current information, there was no outage of the general power supply. Energy provider confirms incident The facility belongs to the energy provider Amprion, which confirmed the incident. “An incident occurred on Tuesday evening in the vicinity of Amprion’s Rommerskirchen substation in the Rhineland that affected the operation of power plant feeders,” the company stated early Wednesday morning. This reportedly led to equipment failures at RWE Power. The Dortmund-based company added: “The general power supply was not affected at any time, and system stability was always ensured.” Experts from Amprion are working with the relevant safety authorities to clarify the facts as quickly as possible and assess the impact. The latest incident comes only a day after a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg. Explosion at Augsburg station Meanwhile, at least two people sustained minor blast injuries in an explosion at a train station in the southern city of Augsburg on Wednesday. The station building and Track 1 were closed, while trains were rerouted and local public transportation was disrupted. Several windowpanes were also damaged. Explosives experts from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office were dispatched to the scene. The cause of the explosion remains unknown. Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant The incidents came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities. Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant. “We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said. Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded. Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated. Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred. Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected. The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All IMO urges member states to stop attacking merchant ships Global markets trade mixed ahead of Fed’s rate decision Yemeni army targets Houthi positions in western Taiz Kosovo's ex-President Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes EU to introduce common age limit for social media EU Commission chief calls for new European Security Council,' bloc-wide emergency security protocol Türkiye, Azerbaijan are '2 islands of stability' in region: Turkish foreign minister See All At least 2 people injured in explosion at German train station, police report France backs sanctions over Leipzig attack, targets Russian shadow fleet: Foreign minister

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/21/trum.text: US President Donald Trump said Washington was working on a "massive" deal to buy fertilizer from Belarus, despite Minsk's repression of dissidents and support for Russia's war in Ukraine.Trump said on social media that the cost of the potash from Belarus would be "substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada," the US neighbour against which he has stepped up a trade war.Potash is a potassium-rich salt mined mainly for fertilizer, helping crops grow and improving yields. Canada supplies most of the potash used by American farmers.Belarus is one of the world's largest producers, but the European Union bans imports of Belarusian potash and has frozen the assets of state producer Belaruskali.The announcement is the latest in a series of deals between Washington and Minsk. Talks led by US envoy John Coale have seen Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko pardon hundreds of political prisoners in exchange for the easing of US sanctions on Belarusian firms, including its potash industry.Belarus remains a close ally of Russia and allowed Moscow to use its territory as a staging ground for the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and more recently authorised joint nuclear drills.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Israel is expected to close British consulate in East Jerusalem this week. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Israel is expected to close British consulate in East Jerusalem this week. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images Israel UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closure Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.53 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 19.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week. This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel . The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright. Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements. Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family Read more The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country. The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem. An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future. “We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.” The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed. It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile. The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this. Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute. Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “We are all concerned because if this (closure of the consulate) goes ahead it would be an incredibly damaging precedent for the status of missions in Jerusalem, which are monitoring the status quo,” said one western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. “It would be inconceivable for the British government to accept (the closure) because they don’t recognise the authority of the Israeli government over Jerusalem under international law. Particularly as Israel is taking this step over British measures which are simply applying international law.” Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine , in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem. France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them. Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements. UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods. The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine. https://www.dw.com/en/north-korean-worke.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OSRJ North Korean state media showed Kim Jong Un inspecting drones at an undisclosed location in North Korea (FILE: September 2026) Image: KCNA/KNS/AFP Advertisement As many as 12,000 North Koreans working at a Russian drone factory are victims of "gross human rights abuses and human trafficking," according to a new report. The figures were part of a joint report published on October 14 by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Dallas-based George W. Bush Institute. It analyzes how Russia, North Korea, China and Iran are involved in expanding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production at the Yelabuga plant in Tatarstan, and what each country stands to gain. While Moscow gets access to more than 5,500 drones a month for its war against Ukraine , China benefits from being the main supplier of dual-use components, including batteries, internal electronics, engines and navigation systems. Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drones , which has helped Moscow produce upgraded domestic variants, known as Geran. Meanwhile, North Korea is earning money by retaining as much as 90% of the wages of the laborers, the report stated. "The geographical locations of these four countries… means that any kind of international interdiction is impossible," Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, told DW. North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Russia and North Korea defy UN resolutions The joint report says Russia and North Korea are defying United Nations Security Council Resolution 2397, of December 2017 , which requires any UN member state to send North Korean workers home within two years. "The North Korean regime… is selling the labor of its citizens under a state-to-state arrangement, controlling whether they may leave and collecting most of their wages," it said. This, according to the report, "is the definition of forced labor." Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist with the Worldwide Coalition to Stop Genocide in North Korea, says Pyongyang is "effectively conducting slavery of its own people and for its own profit." "This is just a terrible situation, and we know that it is not happening only at Yelabuga," he told DW. "We know there are construction workers in the occupied Ukrainian territories, North Koreans in lumber camps and, of course, tens of thousands of soldiers have been sent to fight — and die — on the front lines in Ukraine ," Song added. " Life in North Korea is not easy , but these people are being sent to Russia as slaves, with no freedom, and they are only allowed to keep a fraction of the money they earn," he said. The challenge, he admits, is to find a way to halt this "trade in humanity." North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How much can realistically be done? "These countries share a border, so it is easy to transport workers, and no other agency can intervene," Song said. "Russia and China are both permanent members of the UN Security Council but are ignoring its resolutions on this issue. There is very little that can be done." Song's rights organization is attempting to highlight the plight of North Korean workers and to create a "coalition of like-minded nations and agencies" to protect laborers — although he admits to being "pessimistic." Pinkston shares those concerns, as well as fears over the emergence of a powerful bloc that appears to be "ripping up the post-World War II order on the rule of law and human rights " and is intent on taking a confrontational approach to other nations. The weapons being manufactured at Yelabuga will assist in achieving those aims, he said. "UN Security Council resolutions on North Korean workers, on weapons proliferation, on the sale of dual-use technologies are all being ignored, so I think we can say that the UN's sanctions regime is pretty much dead," Pinkston added. North Korea developing its drone capabilities It is clear that both Russia and Ukraine have gained important insights into the modern battlefield through their ongoing conflict, Pinkston said, with the emergence of drone technology arguably one of the most critical advances. "And like everyone else, North Korea has been watching closely, 'learning-by-doing' and innovating its own drone capabilities," Pinkston said, adding that there are "serious implications" for the South Korean military as it also attempts to keep up its defensive capabilities against a new generation of drones in the North . Why Russia and North Korea can't quit each other (for now) To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video To curb the deployment of North Korean laborers to Russia and the proliferation of weapons, the joint report calls on the US State Department to work with other countries to disrupt human trafficking networks and sanction those responsible. It also urges the UN to work multilaterally to investigate the Yelabuga complex and to catalogue the abuses that have taken place. Moreover, it demands accountability for those who have carried out abuses and for victims to be protected. The report adds that foreign companies that are operating as part of the Yelabuga special economic zone — there are "several" European companies and at least one US firm with a presence at the site — should be pressured to leave.
